hints.title: Use a convenient whole-number model
hints.body: Use a model with 25 club members. Then 60% gives 15 women, leaving 10 men. Keep separate counts for men/women and tennis/cricket.
hints.recap: Turn proportions into counts while keeping the group totals distinct.
hints.pitfall: The fractions refer to different groups; label each group before multiplying.
hints.pause: How many of the 10 men play cricket?

recall.reminder: A conditional fraction uses the people in its stated group as its denominator.

hints.title: Use the cricket group as its own whole
hints.body: The given fraction of cricketers who are women also determines the fraction who are men. Compare that fraction with your number of male cricketers.
hints.recap: A conditional fraction must use its stated group as the whole.
hints.pitfall: The fraction of cricketers who are women is not the fraction of women who play cricket.
hints.pause: Recover the cricket group, find the women who play tennis and express their count as a fraction of the whole club.

recall.reminder: A conditional fraction must use its stated group as the whole.

solution:
1. Set up the counts. In a 25-member model, 15 members are women and 10 are men. Male cricketers number 25×10=4.

2. Use the cricket ratio. Women are 23 of the cricket group, so the four men are its remaining 13. There must be 8 female cricketers.

3. Return to the whole-club sample space. There are 15−8=7 women tennis players. The probability is 725: answer B. Scaling the model changes every count by the same factor and leaves this probability unchanged.
